title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with prices on everything: a bed, a boxed meal, a phone, a lawyer's fee — all bought with cash, and those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series — medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who raise prices on the spot — is the part actually worth your time.
who: Founders and going-global operators interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the machinery of gray industry and immigration corruption.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: Immigration quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, an immigration officer pulled him aside and quietly said, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the word came back: hand over 1.5 million pesos, roughly 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you walk immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 or 13 people picked up in the same sweep, nobody agreed to pay — everyone thought something like this couldn't possibly still exist in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal channels. The price of refusing: they were moved from the holding cells of the General Santos police station to the immigration headquarters detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code; he assumed this was standard procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and could not get the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and it was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — then sent back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili says it isn't about the amount; it's that the phone was out of his hands and someone touched it. His read: many Chinese in Manila doing gray-industry scams who get arrested go through this same shakedown, but they don't dare approach the Chinese consulate, because their phones are full of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the immigration office promised exist — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own ticket to transfer, immigration works on them in shifts, saying the Manila immigration facility is in great condition, has air conditioning, is very free — you can work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili says they weren't lying: there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout — just in a completely different form. They arrived at the headquarters detention center after 3 a.m.; what he saw getting out of the vehicle was a square area wrapped in a layer of iron grating under a sheet-metal roof, ringed by dog-cage-like iron cells, and inside, one long communal platform bed holding several hundred people. At 3 a.m. many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the iron cages staring at the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners said nothing for several minutes, then it hit them: immigration had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss in cooperation with immigration, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The cheapest tier, a spot on the communal platform bed, was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan bosses and gambling kingpins could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bunk. That is where immigration's promise of "air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, that he was here to serve time — how could he be expected to pay on top of that? The gang boss, threatening, said: you're already in here and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run through gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes everything for Chinese inmates — food, clothing, daily life — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the off season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff draw wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 — very low pay, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer and can only work to earn.

points.h: A man from Yunnan held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom scams, and when his numbers were bad his supervisor shocked him with a stun baton every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation process is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you leave — but immigration, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the process doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Immigration afterward bought a basic feature phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese Feili talked with much came from a scam company whose 70 or 80 people were surrounded by immigration together with the police and the NBI, three agencies at once. The first shakedown: the NBI and police locked each person in a toilet — because there are no cameras in the toilets — and took everything valuable off them. The second: immigration negotiated with the company boss over ransoms, with different quotes per person — 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos — depending on the mood of the person in charge. That company's deal was 3 million pesos a head, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB and bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was hit with an illegal gun-possession charge by a dirty cop — which is why he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raises the price on the spot when he sees you're Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, to get it done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price was another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the genuinely reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedural pipeline inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held a little over 30 days, 41 including Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.

quotes.text: If you give him 1.5 million pesos now, he can let you out immediately, and you won't have any problem at all.
But it's not about how much money it was — when the phone wasn't in my hands, it was transferred out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and his ordinary people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are fundamentally very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — the kind of bureaucratic system that drinks blood, human blood.
